# What Is Fit to Call Self?

*SN 22.59, the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta — set 4, Not-Self and Dependent Arising*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 6 min · 1,016 words</p>

## Before you read

<div class="reader-guide" markdown="1">

### What happens

At the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī, the Buddha asks five monks about five categories of experience.

### Central question

Is it reasonable to say of any of these five changing parts of experience, 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?

### Main point

Each of the five can cause trouble, changes over time, and cannot be made to obey your wishes. So the text says none is fit to be treated as 'mine,' 'I am this,' or 'my self.' It connects seeing this clearly with release.

### Reading tip

The same argument is repeated for all five categories. Use the first one to learn the pattern. Later, watch for the repeated line: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

### This text is not saying

This passage is not trying to prove that nobody exists. It focuses on whether these five changing parts of experience are fit to be treated as 'mine,' 'I am this,' or 'my self.'

### Key words

<p class="reader-guide__terms-intro">These definitions are here so you do not need to know Pali or Buddhist vocabulary before reading.</p>
<dl class="reader-guide__terms">

<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;rūpa&quot; -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>felt experience</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;vedanā&quot; (often translated &quot;feeling&quot;) -- the immediate pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral tone of an experience, prior to any story built on top of it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>recognition</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saññā&quot; (often translated &quot;perception&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.</dd>
<dt><dfn>putting-together activities</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saṅkhārā&quot; (often translated &quot;mental formations&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s constructing and assembling activity, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>not-self</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;anattā&quot; -- not a claim that you don&#x27;t exist, but that nothing in experience holds up as a fixed, ownable &quot;self&quot; when actually examined.</dd>
</dl>

## Translation

### The Setting

So I heard.

At one time the Buddha was staying near Bārāṇasī, at Isipatana, in the Deer
Park.

There the Buddha addressed the group of five bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus."

"Bhante," they replied.

The Buddha said this:

### The Five Heaps Are Not-Self

"Bhikkhus, form is not-self.

For if form were self, form would not lead to affliction, and it would be
possible to say of form: 'May my form be like this; may my form not be like
that.'

But because form is not-self, form leads to affliction, and it is not
possible to say of form: 'May my form be like this; may my form not be like
that.'

Felt experience is not-self.

For if felt experience were self, felt experience would not lead to
affliction, and it would be possible to say of felt experience: 'May my felt
experience be like this; may my felt experience not be like that.'

But because felt experience is not-self, felt experience leads to affliction,
and it is not possible to say of felt experience: 'May my felt experience be
like this; may my felt experience not be like that.'

Recognition is not-self.

For if recognition were self, recognition would not lead to affliction, and it
would be possible to say of recognition: 'May my recognition be like this; may
my recognition not be like that.'

But because recognition is not-self, recognition leads to affliction, and it
is not possible to say of recognition: 'May my recognition be like this; may
my recognition not be like that.'

Putting-together activities are not-self.

For if putting-together activities were self, putting-together activities
would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible to say of
putting-together activities: 'May my putting-together activities be like this;
may my putting-together activities not be like that.'

But because putting-together activities are not-self, putting-together
activities lead to affliction, and it is not possible to say of
putting-together activities: 'May my putting-together activities be like this;
may my putting-together activities not be like that.'

Knowing is not-self.

For if knowing were self, knowing would not lead to affliction, and it would
be possible to say of knowing: 'May my knowing be like this; may my knowing
not be like that.'

But because knowing is not-self, knowing leads to affliction, and it is not
possible to say of knowing: 'May my knowing be like this; may my knowing not
be like that.'"

### Impermanence, Dissatisfactoriness, And Not-Self

"What do you think, bhikkhus? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, bhante."

"And what is impermanent: is it dissatisfaction or happiness?"

"Dissatisfaction, bhante."

"And what is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject to change: is it fit to
regard it like this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, bhante."

"Is felt experience permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, bhante."

"And what is impermanent: is it dissatisfaction or happiness?"

"Dissatisfaction, bhante."

"And what is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject to change: is it fit to
regard it like this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, bhante."

"Is recognition permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, bhante."

"And what is impermanent: is it dissatisfaction or happiness?"

"Dissatisfaction, bhante."

"And what is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject to change: is it fit to
regard it like this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, bhante."

"Are putting-together activities permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, bhante."

"And what is impermanent: is it dissatisfaction or happiness?"

"Dissatisfaction, bhante."

"And what is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject to change: is it fit to
regard it like this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, bhante."

"Is knowing permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, bhante."

"And what is impermanent: is it dissatisfaction or happiness?"

"Dissatisfaction, bhante."

"And what is impermanent, dissatisfactory, and subject to change: is it fit to
regard it like this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, bhante."

### The De-appropriation Refrain

"So then, bhikkhus, any kind of form there is, past, future, or present,
internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near:
all form should be seen with right discernment as it has come to be: 'This is
not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

Any kind of felt experience there is, past, future, or present, internal or
external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all felt
experience should be seen with right discernment as it has come to be: 'This
is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

Any kind of recognition there is, past, future, or present, internal or
external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all
recognition should be seen with right discernment as it has come to be: 'This
is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

Any kind of putting-together activities there are, past, future, or present,
internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near:
all putting-together activities should be seen with right discernment as they
have come to be: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

Any kind of knowing there is, past, future, or present, internal or external,
coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near: all knowing should be
seen with right discernment as it has come to be: 'This is not mine, I am not
this, this is not my self.'"

### Disenchantment, Fading, And Release

"Seeing this, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with
form, felt experience, recognition, putting-together activities, and knowing.

Being disenchanted, they fade. Through fading, they are released.

When it is released, there is the knowledge: 'It is released.'

They discern: 'Birth is worn away, the spiritual life has been lived, what had
to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"

That is what the Buddha said.

The group of five bhikkhus were glad and welcomed what the Buddha said.

And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of the group of five
bhikkhus were released from the outflows through not taking anything
personally.

<summary>Words used in this translation (17)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>Bhante</dfn></dt>
<dd>A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly &quot;venerable sir.&quot; Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>birth</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jāti&quot; -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.</dd>
<dt><dfn>disenchantment</dfn></dt>
<dd>A cooling of fascination with ordinary experience -- not depression, but the natural next step once you see clearly how things actually work.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dissatisfaction</dfn></dt>
<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>
<dt><dfn>fading</dfn></dt>
<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>
<dt><dfn>felt experience</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;vedanā&quot; (often translated &quot;feeling&quot;) -- the immediate pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral tone of an experience, prior to any story built on top of it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>form</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;rūpa&quot; -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>heaps</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;khandhā&quot; (usually translated &quot;aggregates&quot;) -- the five piles experience gets sorted into: form, felt experience, recognition, putting-together activities, and knowing.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>noble disciple</dfn></dt>
<dd>Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.</dd>
<dt><dfn>not-self</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;anattā&quot; -- not a claim that you don&#x27;t exist, but that nothing in experience holds up as a fixed, ownable &quot;self&quot; when actually examined.</dd>
<dt><dfn>outflows</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;āsavā&quot; -- deep-running habits that keep seeping out and driving behaviour, classically sensuality, becoming, and ignorance. Often translated &quot;taints&quot; or &quot;defilements.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>putting-together activities</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saṅkhārā&quot; (often translated &quot;mental formations&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s constructing and assembling activity, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>recognition</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saññā&quot; (often translated &quot;perception&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.</dd>
<dt><dfn>spiritual life</dfn></dt>
<dd>The Buddhist path of practice as a whole -- not just a set of beliefs, but a whole way of living.</dd>
<dt><dfn>This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self</dfn></dt>
<dd>A three-part formula used throughout these texts to work through attachment to any given piece of experience: not owned by me, not identical with me, not a fixed self underlying me.</dd>
</dl>
